1. Stargardt (ABCA4-associated) macular dystrophy — Most likely given bilateral progressive central loss over years with hyperautofluorescent round/pisciform foci on FAF and subretinal/outer retinal ovoid lesions with hyperreflective borders on OCT; severe asymmetric acuity fits advanced disease.
2. Adult-onset vitelliform (foveomacular) dystrophy — Presents with round hyperautofluorescent subretinal deposits and characteristic ovoid hyperreflective material on OCT producing marked central vision loss; can be adult-onset and bilateral.
3. Cone–rod dystrophy — Explains combined central and peripheral visual decline and severe acuity loss; would be supported if full-field ERG shows predominant cone dysfunction and color vision is impaired.
4. Pattern dystrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (including butterfly or multifocal pattern dystrophy) — Can produce hyperautofluorescent flecks and subretinal deposits with progressive central vision loss, typically adult-onset.
5. Geographic atrophy/advanced macular degeneration or central areolar choroidal dystrophy — Less likely given age and lesion appearance but can produce hyperautofluorescent borders and outer retinal loss with severe acuity decline.

Recommended next steps to confirm diagnosis (for your clinician to order): fluorescein angiography (look for “silent/choroidal” fundus in Stargardt), ABCA4 genetic testing, full-field and multifocal ERG, color vision testing and formal Humphrey visual fields, and repeat detailed dilated fundus exam with fundus photography/OCT-A.
